newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia to stage mass evacuation from Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: Australia to stage mass evacuation from Cambodia.

text.p: Australia will on Friday begin the evacuation of hundreds of Australians, Canadians and New Zealanders from strife-torn Cambodia, Foreign Minister Alexander Downer announced on Thursday.

Downer also said Australia was reviewing its A$32 million (US$24 million) annual aid and military assistance to Cambodia and urged co-premier Hun Sen to return democracy to the Southeast Asian nation.
Downer said that while the situation in the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh was calm, Australia had decided to offer evacuation because of growing fears among its nationals.
"While the situation in the Cambodian capital is now realitvely calm, members of the Australian community are understandably concerned about future uncertainty," he said.
Australia on Thursday issued a travel advisory recommending all nationals without essential duties in Cambodia leave, but it was not withdrawing its own diplomats.

There are up to 600 Australians in Cambodia, but foreign affairs officials reckoned that only 400 Australians and foreigners would take up the evacuation offer. Australia has offered spare seats to American, German and British nationals and any Swedish nationals would also be evacuated.

Five Australian military C-130 transport aircraft were available for "Operation Vista", two of them already on standby in Malaysia. A sixth plane was to fly from New Zealand to the northern Australian city of Darwin on Friday as back-up.
"This airlift will help make sure than everyone who wants to leave can," New Zealand Foreign Minister Don McKinnon said in Wellington.
The first aircraft was expected to land in Phnom Penh on Friday morning.
Hundreds of Thai and Singaporean nationals have already been evacuated from Cambodia and the United States has said it would be pulling out about 40 diplomats and dependents.
Washington has also urged between 1,000 and 1,300 other Americans in Phnom Penh and elsewhere in Cambodia to leave over the next few days.

Downer condemned Hun Sen's military ousting of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, expressed anger at reports that Hun Sen's opponents were being attacked and urged an immediate end to the violence followed by fair elections.
"It is of great concern to us that the elections are held, as they're sheduled to be held in May next year, and that those elections are open and fair elections," Downer said.

Downer said Australia was discussing with United Nations Security Council members a coordinated international response to Cambodia, but hinted Australian aid to Cambodia could be at risk if democracy did not return to the country.

"It is time for Australia to be talking to other aid donors about Cambodia, but we have made no decisions yet in terms of our aid programme. Nor have we made any decisions yet in relation to our defence cooperation programme," he said.
"But those matters, naturally enough, will be considered."
Australia is Cambodia's fourth largest aid donor.

Downer also said Australia had expressed its concern about the situation in Cambodia to members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the regional body due to admit Cambodia this month.
But he said Australia had stopped short of asking ASEAN to delay Cambodia's entry. "We don't get into telling ASEAN what to do or what not to do in terms of the membership of ASEAN."
"But, nevertheless, we have made the point to the ASEAN governments that what really matters in this exercise is the return to a proper, appropriate, constitutional government in Cambodia."
ASEAN states on Thursday began an emergency meeting in Kuala Lumpur to discuss the Cambodian crisis.
